i01: That said, the power to remove somebody is also one of the easiest powers to abuse. So work out the process before it's about anyone in particular. What conduct constitutes a reason for immediate protective action, and who decides on temporary restrictions? Who preserves the evidence, and who has to step aside from the decisions? How does the person reply, and what review or appeal is possible without endangering others? How do people who are separated get housed, have their records and family connections protected, and still be able to use common resources or have access to outside funds, if any? When do people reach for outside help? (More on that one next.)
i02: Also pick a mediator or ombud beforehand. Why bother? Because if they are chosen in a crisis, and nobody has met this “neutral stranger” before, people often do not trust them. And remember that although mediation is for repairing relations, it does not replace the need for evidence, safeguarding or a ruling. And it does not replace the finality of separation once someone no longer consents to the shared life.
